    • ideas

    • drillShare

      public float drillShare
      Share of this stage's fights that are combo drills. A fighter that wins most of its exchanges is rarely on the wrong end of a combo and so never learns to get out of one. In a drill the opponent is a saved copy of the agent itself, which combos as well as the agent does; it starts right in front of the agent and is given its first hits before the agent gets its keys back. The agent then starts where it otherwise seldom is: some hits into the opponent's combo.

    • critDrillShare

      public float critDrillShare
      Share of this stage's fights that are crit drills instead: twenty seconds with an opponent that stands still close by and does not hit back. Jumping, coming down with the sprint off and swinging on the way down is hard enough to find without an opponent that moves and hits; here there is nothing else to do. Nothing from these counts towards passing the stage.

    • critDrillPass

      public float critDrillPass
      Above zero: the crit drills come first and alone, one lesson after another (see Curriculum.DRILL_RANGE and the one after it). Every fight of the stage is a drill of the lesson it is at until that lesson is passed; only after the last do the stage's own fights begin (and the drills drop to critDrillShare). Until then the stage's own count of steps does not move, and the stage cannot be passed.

      This is what the first lesson asks: the share of the hits it lands on the standing opponent that have to be critical.

    • critDrillKeep

      public float critDrillKeep
      Once the lessons are passed and the first drill only goes on among the fights: the share of its hits there that still have to be critical for it to count as kept. Lower than what the lesson asks: in the fights it learns when a jump is not worth making, and brings some of that back to the drill. Zero: the same as the lesson.

    • critDrillFirstKept

      public boolean critDrillFirstKept
      Whether the first drill has to stay passed for the stage to be passed. False: it is a lesson, passed once, and goes on among the fights so that the jump stays something it can do; whether it then jumps is left to what its fights pay. (0.14.0: against an opponent a sprint hit knocks away a jump loses more hits than its critical hit is worth, and it stops jumping there within fifty updates, in the drill as well. The stage could then never be passed.)

    • critDrillFarJumpMax

      public float critDrillFarJumpMax
      Above zero, the first lesson also asks this: of the ticks it stands with the opponent out of reach, the largest share on which it may still jump. (What the lesson was about in 0.13.1 to 0.13.3, when a jump was only wanted from right in the opponent's face.)

    • critDrillPunishPass

      public float critDrillPunishPass
      The second lesson asks this: of the hits that knock it up and leave the opponent in its reach as it comes down, the share it answers with a critical hit made from that fall (a punish crit).

    • drillFromSprintHits

      public float drillFromSprintHits
      The drills only run while the agent's own recent fights in this stage show it can combo: at least this share of its hits are sprint hits and its combos are at least this long on average. Until then its copy cannot combo either, so there is no combo to get out of, and being hit by an equal a quarter of the time would only teach a fighter that has never been hit to keep away. Zero: no such condition (it has already shown it in an earlier stage).

    • jumpNudgeRate

      public float jumpNudgeRate
      Above zero: while this stage is young the policy is pushed towards jumping right after a swing (see JumpNudge), as strongly as it takes for it to press jump on this share of those ticks. Held there for jumpNudgeHoldSteps steps of the stage, then let down to nothing by jumpNudgeSteps; from then on it jumps of its own accord or not at all.

    • jumpNudgeHoldSteps

    • backNudgeRate

      public float backNudgeRate
      The same for S in the ticks right after a hit of a combo it is taking (see BackNudge): the share of those ticks on which the stage wants S held while it pushes for it, how long it holds that, and by when the push is gone.

    • backNudgeKeep

      public float backNudgeKeep
      Above zero: the push towards S in the ticks after a hit of a combo does not end with backNudgeSteps (or, in a stage without such a stretch, is there from its start). It is kept at whatever it takes for S to be held on this share of those ticks, in training and in every fight it plays.

      Not a lesson but a habit it is given, like the rule about the sword's charge. Measured (0.14.0, against a copy of itself that had a combo going on it): with the push held it was out by the opponent's second hit in two combos of three and the drill paid 0.085 a step; as the push was let down it was out of one in two and then one in three, the drill paid 0.04, and by the end S was held on none of those ticks. The move works and the network does not keep it: one escape model answers every opponent, and against the one that runs straight back in, backing off gains nothing. Left to itself it drops the move everywhere.

    • lessonChangedIn

      public int lessonChangedIn
      The config version in which what this stage teaches last changed so much that a fighter which passed it before has not learned it. A run saved under older rules that is in a later scripted stage goes back to this one.

    • lagTicks

      public int lagTicks
      Largest lag, in ticks, in what the opponent (the scripted bot or a copy) sees of the agent: each fight draws its own, anywhere from none to this many ticks. A fighter that has only ever fought with no delay at all is lost on a server.

    • seenLagTicks

      public int seenLagTicks
      Largest lag, in ticks, in what the agent sees of its opponent, drawn per fight in the same way. On a server this is the longer of the two: a hit knocks the opponent up only once the hit has gone to the server, on to the opponent's game, and its answer has come all the way back.

    • lagStutter

      public float lagStutter
      In half of the fights the opponent also reaches the agent's eyes in fits and starts, as over a connection that stutters: on each tick, with a chance of up to this much (drawn per fight), nothing arrives for LAG_STALL_MIN_TICKS to LAG_STALL_MAX_TICKS ticks and then all of it at once. 0: never.

    • hitLagTicks

      public int hitLagTicks
      Largest lag, in ticks, of the opponent's own connection, drawn per fight: a hit knocks it back that many ticks late, and until then it goes on as it was, still in reach and able to swing. A combo learned on an opponent that flies off the moment it is hit does not work on one that does not.

    • knockbackMin

      public float knockbackMin
      Between 0 and 1: in every other fight the opponent is knocked back less far than a hit would throw it, by a share drawn per fight between this and all of it. A real opponent takes less than the full knockback much of the time: it is running into the hit, or it jumps as it lands. A combo that only works on an opponent thrown the full distance every time does not work on that one. 0: always the full knockback.

    • pathLagTicks

      public int pathLagTicks
      Above zero: each fight draws one connection for the whole way between the two fighters, and that is used for all three of lagTicks, seenLagTicks and hitLagTicks, whose own values are then not used. This is the most the opponent's connection takes one way, in ticks, in an ordinary fight: none to this many, short ones more often (see Trainer.drawPathLag).

      On a server the three are one thing. A hit moves the opponent only once it has gone to the opponent's own game and that game's answer has come back: its connection there and back, so twice the way. Until then the server has it walking on as it was, in reach and able to swing. And what either fighter sees of the other is old by the opponent's way plus the fighter's own (none or one tick, drawn per fight). Drawn separately and small (up to 0.13.3: seen 0 to 4 late, hit 0 to 2 late), the knockback was never more than two ticks late, so the fighter had hardly met an opponent that stays where it is while the sword recharges. Against one that did, it swung again at once.

    • slowShare

      public float slowShare
      The share of this stage's fights that are against an opponent on a slow connection: a hit knocks it back between slowKnockbackMinTicks and slowKnockbackMaxTicks ticks late (a quarter to half a second), and each sees the other half of that late. Needs pathLagTicks.

      The rest are the ordinary ones, where the knockback is none to four ticks late. A fighter has to be able to fight both and cannot be told which it has in front of it: it finds out from its first hit, by whether the opponent goes when it is hit or a third of a second later. (0.14.0, first runs: one draw for all fights, none to six ticks, short ones more often; one fight in six had the knockback five ticks late or more, and none more than six. Against a player whose knockback took 0.3 to 0.5 seconds it was lost.)

    • fairShare

      public float fairShare
      Against a copy of itself: the share of the fights that are set up on equal terms, and they are the ones that count as won or lost. Nothing is late for either of them, the copy is knocked back as far as the fighter is, what the fighter sees of it does not stutter, and they start facing each other. In every other fight of such a stage something is against the fighter and nothing against the copy: the copy's knockback comes late or carries it less far, which keeps it in reach; what the fighter sees of it comes in fits and starts; the copy starts with its eyes on the fighter and the fighter has to find it. Those are what it is to learn to deal with, and who wins them says what they are worth, not which of the two is the better. (Counted without this, a fighter put against a copy of itself made that very minute lost 16 of 19.)

    • traderShare

      public float traderShare
      Share of this stage's own fights that are against a trader: the stage's opponent, but one that cannot be kept away. It keeps pushing in, it is ready to swing traderReactionTicks ticks after it has the fighter in reach, and a hit throws it back only a part of the way (drawn per fight between traderKnockbackMin and traderKnockbackMax), so it is back before the fighter's sword is.

      This is the opponent a critical hit is for. Against one that a sprint hit sends flying, a combo of sprint hits is simply the better fight: it is hit and cannot hit back. Measured (0.14.0, the first fights after the crit drills): jumping for a third of its hits, the fighter landed 49 hits a minute and took 45; with the jump left alone, 69 and 22. It dropped the jump, and it was right to. But an opponent that takes the hit and stays (one that runs into the hit, jumps as it lands, or is a quarter of a second away on a server) trades hit for hit whatever is done, and then the only question is whose hits do more. So: knock back the opponent that can be knocked back, and crit the one that cannot.

    • runnerShare

      public float runnerShare
      The share of the stage's own fights that are against a runner: the stage's opponent, but one that keeps running out of the fight (BotProfile.fleeChance). And the share against a circler: one that goes round the fighter and makes its hits as jumped critical hits (BotProfile.orbit). What they are for: against every opponent up to 0.14.0 a jump was the wrong call, since each of them either swung at whatever came into its reach or could not be kept off at all, and so the fighter stopped jumping. A player who runs is caught by a running jump and not by a run, and the hit to make on one is a critical hit; one who circles and crits leaves a punish crit to make after every hit, to a fighter that can keep its crosshair on it.

      public float backerShare
      And against one that does what this fighter did until then: hit, it walks backwards for twelve ticks with its eyes on the fighter and its sword ready. That is the opponent the running jump and the critical hit on the way down are for (JumpIn.chaseInCombo): where the fighter practises on someone else what was done to it.

    • timerShare

      public float timerShare
      And against one that plays on its rhythm: it holds a step outside its reach and times its critical hits to come down just before the fighter's sword is back (BotProfile.timer). What the user's friend still beat it with on 18 October.

    • spacerShare

      public float spacerShare
      And against the player at the edge of the reach (BotProfile.spacer): one that comes in with a jump for a critical hit and backs out with S straight after, one that stands three blocks off and hits whatever comes into its reach, perfectly, and one that does both. A third of the fights each.

    • whifferShare

      public float whifferShare
      And against the player spacing beats: it walks in and swings the moment its sword is back, on rhythm, whether or not the fighter is quite in reach. Held off at the edge of the reach it misses, and its cooldown is the opening. Where the fighter learns to space others, not only to get out of being spaced. The user, 18 October: "I WANT IT TO LEARN TO ALSO kill some ppl with this method".

    • peopleShare

      public float peopleShare
      And against scripted copies of real players it has fought in /swordai fight: their habits, counted from those fights, played out by the script (PersonStyle). The players it lost to, or nearly, come up most. Where there are none yet, these fights are against the stage's own opponent.

    • opponentJumpReset

      public float opponentJumpReset
      Each scripted opponent of this stage jumps with this share of the hits it takes; see BotProfile.jumpResetChance.

    • besideShare

      public float besideShare
      The share of the fights against one that goes round the fighter, or takes no knockback, that begin with it close by and off to a side or behind: out of the picture, and making its first critical hit from there.

    • randomShare

      public float randomShare
      The share of the fights against a scripted opponent in which that opponent is not the stage's as written but one drawn afresh: how quick it is, how well it aims, how near it likes to be, how often it jumps, backs off or comes in for a critical hit.

    • circlerCrit

      public float circlerCrit
      The share of a circler's swings that are jumped critical hits.
